By integrating spectral characteristics with spatio-temporal dependencies through feature propagation across consecutive temporal observations, FP-xLSTM effectively captured short-term fluctuations and learned vertical distribution patterns of heterogeneous WQPs from multi-source data while reducing sampling requirements. A field study with an eight-month interval between the first and last sampling campaigns was conducted to evaluate the proposed framework under cross-region experimental settings and against state-of-the-art baseline models. Results demonstrated that FP-xLSTM consistently outperformed competing methods, achieving average coefficients of determination (R2) ranging from 0.66 to 0.95 and mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) between 9.33% and 19.06%. Furthermore, the framework has potential for deployment in practical environmental monitoring applications to support local environmental authorities in tracking river water quality dynamics and optimizing management strategies. Overall, the proposed method provided an effective and scalable intelligent framework for UAV-assisted urban water quality assessment and multi-depth environmental visualization.

title: SDFNet: Snow Depth Retrieval Based on a Multi-Scale Feature Fusion Network for the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
summary: High-resolution snow depth (SD) information supports hydrological and cryospheric studies in complex mountain regions. Coarse SD products limit representation of terrain-related snow variability in these environments. This study proposes SDFNet, a Snow Depth Fusion Network combining Sentinel-1 SAR, Landsat optical data, digital elevation model (DEM) variables, and fractional snow cover (FSC). Multi-scale feature extraction, channel enhancement, and feature aggregation modules represent relationships among these inputs. Observations from 95 meteorological stations across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau supplied supervision and reference measurements for evaluation. Station SD was the regression target rather than a prediction input. In the station-based comparison, SDFNet achieved an RMSE of 5.246 cm and an R2 of 0.702. It had the lowest RMSE and highest R2 among the compared models. However, SD above 40 cm produced an RMSE of 21.927 cm and a bias of −16.061 cm, indicating substantial deep-snow underestimation. Sparse station coverage limits inference beyond the sampled environments, and independent spatial validation remains necessary.

title: Wave as Disturbance and Signal in a Physics-Informed Framework for Shallow Water Bathymetry
summary: Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) commonly treats the sea surface as a source of radiometric disturbance, although the same surface wave field can also contain water depth information through gravity wave propagation. This article presents a Wave-Aware Physics-Informed Neural Network (WA-PINN) that represents these two roles within a unified shallow water bathymetry framework. The optical geometry stream combines Sentinel-2 multispectral observations with seafloor geometry. The disturbance stream converts European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis Version 5 (ERA5) wind forcing into Mean Square Slope (MSS) through the Cox–Munk relationship and introduces a roughness-dependent sunglint contribution into the optical physics constraint. The signal stream retrieves local wavelength, propagation direction, and wave celerity from Sentinel-2 surface texture and constrains predicted depth with the finite depth gravity wave dispersion relation. A Wave Validity Factor (WVF) controls the influence of the dispersion constraint according to the coherence and physical plausibility of the retrieved wave field. The three streams are fused in a shared depth predictor constrained by supervised depth loss, optical physics loss, and wave dispersion physics loss. The framework is demonstrated over Culebra, St. Thomas, and St. John in the northeastern Caribbean Sea. The complete Dual Role model reaches an overall Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 1.21 m, a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) 0.77 m, and an R2 of 0.96. Relative to the Slope Aware configuration, the Disturbance and Signal models reduce RMSE by 15.7% and 12.8%, while the complete model reduces RMSE by 29.7%. The disturbance contribution increases under stronger wind forcing, whereas the signal contribution increases with WVF. Depth-dependent RMSE increases from 0.82 m at 0 to 5 m to 1.58 m at 20 to 30 m. These results illustrate the intended complementarity between correcting wave-induced optical contamination and exploiting wave propagation as an additional depth constraint.

title: Classification and Remote Sensing Characterization of Large Catastrophic Landslides in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau, China
summary: Large catastrophic landslides in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau are characterized by huge volumes and complex chains that frequently cause river damming and casualties. Based on field surveys, multi-temporal satellite imagery, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) deformation measurements, and meteorological and seismic records, this study classifies these landslides into three types by their initiation and disaster-chain processes: (1) rock–ice avalanche → debris flow → landslide dam; (2) debris flow → landslide dam; (3) rock avalanche → landslide dam. Representative cases illustrate the material sources, initiation settings, and downstream impacts of each type. The occurrence of such landslides is influenced by the interplay of four groups of factors: fractured rock masses and abundant loose deposits provide the material basis; high mountains and narrow river valleys provide the spatial framework for landslide evolution and promote river blockage; pronounced climatic changes provide the background conditions and may affect slope stability in glaciated areas through glacier retreat; and frequent strong earthquakes can both instantaneously trigger failure and cause cumulative damage that predisposes slopes to subsequent failures. Ongoing climate warming and repeated seismic activity are expected to increase landslide susceptibility, highlighting the urgency of multi-hazard early warning and proactive mitigation. This study supports early warning prioritization and risk governance in high-mountain valleys across the Tibetan Plateau.

title: Long-Term Mangrove Dynamics and Environmental Associations in the Sundarbans, Bangladesh: Integrating Remote Sensing, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
summary: Mangrove ecosystems are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic disturbances and climate change, despite providing ecological services, including biodiversity conservation, coastal protection, and blue carbon storage. Long-term evaluations of mangrove dynamics and associated environmental conditions remain limited, particularly in the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world. This study examined the spatiotemporal dynamics of the Sundarbans mangrove ecosystem, Bangladesh, using multi-temporal Landsat imagery (1990–2025), Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Model performance was evaluated using the Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) dataset and spatially blocked holdout validation. Classification accuracy was high (94.56–100%) under internal and spatially blocked validation (93.5–99.8%), whereas comparison with GMW yielded lower accuracies (66.4–95.7%). Change detection showed that mangrove area expanded from 2096.66 km2 in 1990 to 3875.95 km2 in 2025, a net gain of almost 1779.29 km2, with substantial inter-period variability and a pronounced mapped decline between 2000 and 2005. SHAP analysis indicated that the relative contributions of model predictors changed over time, with NDVI contributing more strongly to model predictions in recent years than NDWI and NDMI. Mangrove gain, loss, and net change were statistically associated with cyclone exposure and elevation, while precipitation and river discharge showed less consistent relationships. This study highlights a practical method for monitoring spectral dynamics in vulnerable coastal ecosystems and supports mangrove conservation.

title: Adaptive LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS SLAM Framework for Georeferenced Mapping in Challenging Urban Environments
summary: Maintaining accurate, georeferenced dense maps requires reliable global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) observations to constrain global drift. Degraded observations must be prevented from distorting trajectories and local maps as reception transitions from open sky to urban obstruction and complete signal denial indoors. This study develops and evaluates Dense LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS simultaneous localization and mapping (DLIG-SLAM) to adapt GNSS integration and local mapping as reception conditions change. Built on Dense Multi-Scan Adjustment, the framework estimates the local trajectory and dense map separately from the transformation that connects them to a global coordinate frame. GNSS observations are assessed separately for updating this transformation and correcting the estimator. An online switcher selects among integration strategies according to measurement reliability, estimator readiness, and trajectory consistency. Outdoor–indoor state changes reconfigure local mapping, while voxel size adapts to the observed scan point population. Evaluation was performed on four KITTI driving sequences and an urban canyon outdoor–indoor mission in Toronto, recorded with standalone single-point positioning GNSS. GNSS coupling through an inertial navigation estimate achieved the lowest three-dimensional trajectory root mean square error on three of the four KITTI sequences. Online switching did not consistently outperform fixed integration strategies in the KITTI trajectory evaluation. In the Toronto dataset, inertial navigation-mediated coupling achieved the lowest horizontal georeferencing root mean square error of 1.29 m, while full-navigation factor graph smoothing achieved the lowest three-dimensional georeferencing root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.71 m. Online switching achieved the lowest cloud-to-cloud root mean square distance of 6.1 cm against a terrestrial laser scanning reference within the evaluated facade and ground floor region. Controlled experiments also evaluated the effect of separate GNSS admission paths and global transformation policies. The results support adapting GNSS integration to changing reception conditions and mapping objectives, as stronger coupling did not uniformly improve trajectory accuracy, global placement, and local geometric agreement.

title: High-Resolution Multiscale Seismic Fracture Prediction via Basis Pursuit Frequency Extension-Enhanced Multi-Attribute Fusion
summary: Fractures are important storage spaces and flow pathways in tight reservoirs, but small-scale fractures with weak seismic responses are difficult to characterize with band-limited post-stack seismic data. This study proposes a high-resolution multiscale seismic method for predicting fracture distribution based on basis pursuit frequency extension (BPFE)-enhanced multi-attribute fusion. BPFE represents each trace sparsely on a wedge dictionary built from a zero-phase Morlet wavelet, which is derived from the average dominant frequency of the data. It then re-synthesizes the basis pursuit denoising solution with a time-compressed wavelet, thereby extending the effective bandwidth without estimating the seismic wavelet. Dip-steered third-generation coherence and ant-tracking attributes are subsequently normalized and fused with explicit weights according to their attribute-sensitive scales, and objective rules are provided for selecting the BPFE parameters. Synthetic tests with known reflectivity show that BPFE reproduces the ideal high-resolution section with correlation coefficients of 0.978 (noise-free) and 0.882 (signal-to-noise ratio of 10 dB). BPFE increases the dominant frequency from 30.8 to 49.3 Hz and reduces the tuning thickness from 16 to 11 ms without systematic phase rotation. At 10 dB, it also raises the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for detecting weak bed-confined discontinuities from 0.580 to 0.687, outperforming spectral whitening, spiking deconvolution, inverse-Q filtering and sparse-spike inversion in this respect. Applied to the tight sandstone reservoir in the northeastern Sichuan Basin, the workflow delineates main faults, fault-associated fracture zones and small-scale discontinuities more completely than coherence, ant tracking or their fusion without BPFE, which is consistent with the actual geological understanding. The workflow offers a wavelet-estimation-free approach for characterizing weak-response small-scale fractures, although its generalization requires further field validation.

title: A Lightweight Coastal Litter Segmentation Network with Feature Gating and Multiscale Context for UAV Imagery
summary: Litter stranded on beaches can severely degrade local ecosystems and diminish the tourism value of coastal areas. The integration of deep learning into unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) provides an effective means for the automatic segmentation of coastal litter. However, large variations in litter scale and complex coastal backgrounds lead to relatively low detection accuracy. In addition, most existing detection models require substantial computational resources, which limits their deployment. To address these issues, we constructed a coastal litter segmentation dataset and developed a lightweight segmentation model, CoastalLitterNet. The dataset contains litter objects of different sizes, colors, and shapes, with various backgrounds. In CoastalLitterNet, a Lightweight Asymmetric U-shaped Backbone Network (L-Net) was designed to reduce model complexity, and Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) was introduced to segment litter objects at different scales. A CoastalLitterGate (CLG) was proposed to enhance litter-related features and improve adaptability to complex backgrounds. Comparative experiments showed that the mIoU, IoU1 and F1 of CoastalLitterNet reached 93.95%, 88.42% and 93.85%, respectively. The Params and FLOPs of the model are only 12.90 M and 189.30 G, respectively. The quantitative and qualitative results show that CoastalLitterNet effectively segments litter objects at varying scales and adapts well to complex coastal environments while maintaining a lightweight architecture.

title: Improving Open-Set Recognition in Long-Tailed Underwater Optical Monitoring via Frequency-Shrunk Prototypes and Group-Conditional Risk Calibration
summary: Camera-based underwater optical monitoring enables persistent and non-invasive observation of marine communities, but its automated interpretation is challenged by two coupled uncertainties: the natural long-tailed frequency distribution of observed organisms and the appearance of categories absent from model development. Rare known categories provide insufficient observations for reliably estimating class location and dispersion, whereas dominant categories may form broad acceptance regions that absorb previously unseen organisms. We propose Frequency-Shrunk Prototype and Risk Calibration (FSPRC), a known-only post hoc framework for long-tailed underwater optical monitoring built on an ImageNet-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny. FSPRC regularizes each empirical feature direction toward its corresponding classifier direction and shrinks its intraclass radius toward a frequency-group reference, with both corrections controlled by the number of training observations. Local prototype deviation and global energy evidence are then robustly normalized within the predicted head, middle, or tail group and combined without a trainable fusion module. Independent known-only calibration subsets determine group-conditional rejection thresholds, while held-out categories remain excluded from backbone adaptation, checkpoint selection, geometric estimation, score normalization, and threshold fitting. On the predefined fold-0 leakage-controlled protocols for AQUA20 and the track-disjoint Fish4Knowledge-23 dataset, FSPRC achieves open-set accuracies of 83.31% and 98.19%, open-set classification rate (OSCR) values of 85.96% and 98.96%, and unknown category macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values of 92.62% and 99.55%, respectively. Across exhaustive class-held-out partitions, open-set accuracy is 83.25±0.24% over four AQUA20 folds and 98.18±0.08% over five Fish4Knowledge-23 folds. These results demonstrate that frequency-dependent geometric stabilization and risk calibration can improve the recognition-stage balance between retaining data-scarce known organisms and referring unfamiliar observations for subsequent expert inspection.

title: Label-Free Quantitative Evaluation of Land Cover Segmentation Models for Remote Sensing Imagery: A Context-Aware Model Based on OpenStreetMap and a Digital Surface Model
summary: Segmentation performance is measured against pixel-wise ground truth (GT); without it, that measurement cannot be made. Remote sensing segmentation models are evaluated likewise, yet operational systems receive new unlabeled images, and the properties of those images shift with season, region, and sensor aging. A way to check performance outside the training dataset is needed. We propose quantifying segmentation output without labels, using public geospatial data: a random-forest context-aware model predicts class area composition from OpenStreetMap (OSM) and digital surface model (DSM) statistics. Quantile mapping transforms its output to match the distribution of measured compositions, yielding the expected distribution, and the Label-Free Composition Score (LFCS) is the similarity between that distribution and the composition of the segmentation output. The context-aware model is fitted only to geospatial features and GT compositions from the segmentation model’s training dataset, so the expected distribution is independent of the segmentation model’s structure, parameters, and outputs while depending on that dataset’s GT, class scheme, and composition distribution. The evaluation stage requires no GT labels. To test the method, we saved 430 segmentation model checkpoints from 75 training runs under six controlled training variations, so that the mean intersection over union (mIoU) of each, measured against GT on validation tiles held out of training, was known in advance. These GT mIoU values ranged from 0.04 to 0.69. The models were grouped by GT mIoU in steps of 0.1. Their mean LFCS rose with every step: from 0.474 to 0.937 on held-out images from the same dataset, and from 0.467 to 0.893 on 900 globally distributed unlabeled images. Existing measures that read only a model’s own output tracked GT mIoU less consistently. Rebuilding the entire method reproduced the same behavior on two public datasets with different class schemes, confirming the validity of the method under the conditions tested.

title: Fallen Tree Detection and Mapping from Airborne Laser Scanning Point Clouds Using Physics-Guided Supervoxel Learning
summary: Accurate fallen tree detection from airborne laser scanning (ALS) point clouds is important for forest structural assessment and disturbance monitoring. However, fallen trees remain difficult to extract from operational ALS data because near-ground stems are often fragmented by understory occlusion, uneven sampling, and geometric confusion with shrubs, terrain surfaces, and other low vegetation. This study proposes a physics-guided supervoxel framework for fallen tree detection from ALS point clouds. The framework represents ALS observations as spatially coherent supervoxels and describes each supervoxel using local geometric features, cylindrical morphology, and graph-based neighborhood context. Cylindrical descriptors encode the elongated stem structure of fallen trees, while graph-topological features represent spatial continuity among adjacent supervoxels. A stacking ensemble classifier is trained with SHAP-based feature selection, followed by graph-constrained spatial refinement to improve local label consistency. The framework was trained using 30 plots and evaluated on seven held-out forest plots from the Dutch Actueel Hoogtebestand Nederland 4 (AHN4) dataset, with point densities of 10–15 pts/m2. Using point-level reference labels, the stacking classifier achieved a mean fallen tree F1-score of 83.86% across the test plots, which increased to 85.39% after spatial refinement. Ablation results show that cylindrical descriptors provided the largest gain, improving the fallen tree F1 score by 11.77%. These results indicate that physics-guided supervoxel learning can produce interpretable fallen tree maps from operational ALS data and support subsequent analyses of near-ground forest structure and disturbance effects.

title: CAP-DBNet: A Class-Adaptive Prototype-Guided Dual-Branch Collaborative Network for Remote Sensing Image Semantic Segmentation
summary: High-resolution remote sensing image semantic segmentation faces challenges from large-scale variation, fine boundary preservation, and class imbalance. This paper proposes CAP-DBNet, a compact framework that combines a RepViT M2.3 backbone with a global–local collaborative decoder (GLCD), a class-adaptive hybrid loss (CAHL), and a class-adaptive prototype-guided calibration module (CAPC). CAP-DBNet integrates class-center global and window-local modeling through bidirectional feature exchange, mini-batch class-frequency-aware supervision, and prototype-based residual calibration. Rather than introducing an isolated new attention or prototype mechanism, this work focuses on the coordinated design of these components within an efficient segmentation framework. In five repeated experiments with different random seeds, CAP-DBNet achieves average mIoUs of 85.16%, 88.32%, and 55.75% on Vaihingen, Potsdam, and LoveDA, respectively, improving over the same-backbone LOGCAN++ baseline by 1.43, 1.24, and 1.44 percentage points. Compared with D2LS under our evaluation protocol, CAP-DBNet uses 3.55× fewer parameters and requires 8.35× fewer floating-point operations (FLOPs). These results demonstrate an accuracy-efficiency-oriented global–local and class-adaptive framework for remote sensing semantic segmentation across three public benchmarks.

title: A decade of summer glacier fronts and calved glacier ice distribution in Kongs- and Krossfjorden, Svalbard, observed by Sentinel-1 extra wide swath
summary: A statistical method to map atmospheric exposure is applied on the whole decade (2015–2024) of Sentinel-1 summer acquisitions in Extra Wide Swath mode over Kongs- and Krossfjorden on Svalbard. The consistent daily observations not only allow to statistically define a summer glacier front extent of marine-terminating glaciers but also reveal a new application, which is to detect the summer distribution of calved glacier ice, i.e. icebergs, bergy bits and growlers (IBG). These originate from glacier calving during the sea-ice free period. Summer glacier extent that we define statistically as the area where the glacier prevails more than 95% during summer co-locate well with independent glacier fronts digitized from Sentinel-2 optical imagery. Annual summer IBG distributions are classified into percentage ranges of temporal occurrence, representing the proportion of time IBG are detected in the corresponding pixel location. The ten-year record of mean annual summer IBG-occupied areas is compared to separate estimates of summer glacier frontal ablation for the two glaciers Lillehöökbreen and Kronebreen. The comparison indicates a clear link between mean summer calved ice distribution area and the glaciers' frontal ablation with correlation coefficients (r) of 0.67 and 0.85 for Lillehöökbreen and Kronebreen, respectively. Frontal ablation includes both calving and submarine/subaerial melting at the glacier front and combining this with IBG occurrence estimates may provide new insights into the mass loss ratio between calving and melting. However, the relationship between IBG occurrence distribution and frontal ablation appears to be glacier specific. As this study represents a first attempt to map IBG occurrence distribution and mean IBG occupied area and link that to glacier frontal ablation, further studies and application on other glaciers and fjord systems are required to fully assess the potential and limitations of mapping such IBG distribution as a proxy for glacier calving intensities.

title: From national to global: Mapping global center-pivot irrigated cropland with knowledge-guided data augmentation
summary: Center-pivot irrigated cropland (CPIC) is a large-scale, intensive agricultural irrigation practice with high water-use efficiency. This characteristic enables CPIC to increase crop yields and promote agricultural development, while simultaneously causing groundwater overexploitation and subsequent environmental issues. Mapping the global distribution of CPIC is critical for enhancing water resource management, guiding agricultural policies, and assessing ecological impacts. This study developed a novel methodological framework integrating CPIC prior knowledge into the generation of a global training dataset through designed algorithms, ultimately producing a 2020 global CPIC map (GCMap) based on Landsat imagery. Specifically, we first proposed a shape-prior guided Projection Simulation (PS) to enhance the diversity of national-scale CPIC samples, enabling global CPIC pseudo-label generation through a teacher model. Subsequently, a stratified sampling strategy was implemented to improve sample representativeness across different regions using the pseudo-labels of global CPIC. Furthermore, a dual-temporal correction mechanism was proposed to clean sample labels, ultimately generating high-confidence global training samples. Finally, based on this dataset, a student model was trained using a noise-resistant loss function and deployed on cloud computing platforms to generate the GCMap rapidly. Following Olofsson's design-based stratified sampling and error-matrix framework, we derived statistically rigorous area estimates with explicit 95% confidence intervals and assessed mapping accuracy using the corresponding user's accuracy (UA), producer's accuracy (PA), and overall accuracy (OA) metrics. In comparison with current CPIC products, our GCMap attained a PA of 0.86 ± 0.02, representing a marked reduction in omission errors. Our results show that the global error-adjusted area of CPIC in 2020 was estimated at 18.70 ± 0.42 Mha, representing a 63% increase relative to the previous estimate of 11.5 Mha and revealing substantial underestimation in previous estimates. Geographically, the semi-arid zone has the largest share of CPIC, covering 9.27 ± 0.29 Mha (49.28% of the total), followed by the arid zone (4.69 ± 0.20 Mha, 24.95%) and humid zone (2.99 ± 0.22 Mha, 15.92%). Further analysis indicates that most CPIC is distributed in aquifers with limited underwater recharge. Approximately 15.25 ± 0.87 Mha (82.04%) of CPIC areas are located in regions with recharge rates below 100 mm/year, of which 9.97 ± 0.48 Mha (53.62% of total CPIC) fall within extremely low recharge zones (<20 mm/year). These findings provide an essential foundation for further research on irrigation-groundwater interactions and sustainable policymaking about agricultural development and water usage. Our GCMap inventory is publicly available in an online repository at: https://doi.org/10.12436/GCMap.62.20250711 .

title: Substantial disagreement between satellite- and ground-level nighttime light patterns revealed by SDGSAT-1 and street view imagery
summary: Over the past three decades, nighttime light (NTL) has become one of the most widely used and powerful proxies for characterizing human activities. Despite the recent proliferation of available NTL data from both satellite- and ground-level sensors, intrinsic differences between these two observation approaches can result in distinct NTL brightness patterns (satellite-ground disagreement). Such disagreement, particularly its spatial heterogeneity, represents a critical yet largely overlooked issue in NTL studies, introducing uncertainty into the interpretation and application of NTL observations. Here, by incorporating SDGSAT-1 glimmer imagery and panoramic nighttime street view imagery with geospatial AI approaches, we present a spatially explicit, wall-to-wall investigation into satellite-ground disagreement across Singapore. Specifically, we characterized citywide disagreement and its variation across land-use types, analyzed contributing factors, and assessed its implications for NTL-based applications, reinforced by Monte Carlo-based uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analyses using independent observations from Singapore and Shenzhen, China. Our study revealed substantial and spatially heterogeneous satellite-ground disagreement across Singapore. Relative disagreement averaged 15% ± 13% citywide but reached 42% ± 12% in 13% of the city. Such pronounced heterogeneity was likewise evident across land-use types, with commercial areas standing out for consistently significant disagreement, where ground-level NTL brightness was 29% ± 26% higher than satellite-level NTL brightness. Building morphology, vegetation canopy cover, and sensor spectral response contributed to satellite-ground disagreement, suggestive of distinct mechanisms underlying the identified patterns. Applying satellite- and ground-level NTL data yielded relative differences of at least 115% and 83% in GDP estimation and NTL exposure inequality assessment, respectively. This study sheds new light on satellite-ground disagreement by moving beyond discrete comparisons toward a comprehensive analysis of its heterogeneity and implications, thereby establishing an empirical basis for integrating NTL observations and contributing to more reliable NTL-based applications and evidence-informed policies on sustainable urbanization.

title: Evaluating multi-satellite VIIRS active fire observations as a burned area proxy across North America
summary: Wildfire activity fundamentally regulates terrestrial carbon dynamics and atmospheric emissions, necessitating timely and spatially complete mapping of burned area. Traditional reflectance-based burned area products provide robust spatial records but often have multi-week to multi-month processing latencies that limit near-real-time applications. Active-fire detections provide low-latency observations, but their use as a burned area proxy is constrained by temporal sampling gaps and commission errors associated with sub-pixel fire detection. This study represents one of the first applications to use the full three-satellite Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) constellation, comprising S-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21, to address these limitations. Here, we evaluate how the spatial performance of a cumulative VIIRS active-fire approach varies with temporal sampling, latitude, and fire regime. We developed a VIIRS Cumulative Active Fire (VCAF) approach using the 375-m VIIRS active-fire record across North America from 2012 to 2024, and evaluated its spatial agreement with visually interpreted reference labels and the North American Fire History (NAFH) dataset, using MCD64A1 as a benchmark burned area product. Results from the first full year of the three-satellite configuration (2024) indicate that VCAF had higher spatial agreement than MCD64A1 in parts of the high-latitude domain (>50°N), with particularly high patch-level recall for small reference burned patches (<100 ha) while maintaining high recall for large patches (>1000 ha). The observed performance varied substantially with latitude and fire regime. In high-latitude boreal regions, the greater potential sampling frequency of the VIIRS constellation was associated with lower omission errors and greater spatial completeness in some regions, although environmental conditions such as persistent cloud cover remained important limitations. In contrast, VCAF systematically overestimated burned area in fragmented lower-latitude fire regimes. These results indicate that multi-satellite VIIRS active-fire observations can provide a potentially useful burned area proxy in selected high-latitude fire regimes and highlight the importance of accounting for temporal sampling and fire-regime characteristics when interpreting active-fire-based burned area estimates.

title: Divergent transpiration regulation among 20 urban tree species under extreme heat revealed by UAV multisource remote sensing
summary: Urban areas face increasing extreme heat risk, yet satellite remote sensing struggles to quantify crown-scale transpiration in heterogeneous urban landscapes. Consequently, species-specific heat responses, key regulatory factors, and tipping points of urban tree transpiration remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) multispectral, thermal infrared, and LiDAR observations with field surveys of 665 trees across 20 species to estimate crown-scale transpiration for nearly 50,000 trees. The UAV-based single-source energy balance model captured diurnal evapotranspiration (ET) dynamics and agreed well with eddy covariance measurements (R 2 = 0.86, RMSE = 0.04 mm h −1 ). At the individual-tree scale, UAV-derived crown-scale transpiration agreed closely with sap-flow-derived transpiration (R 2 = 0.88, RMSE = 0.05 mm h −1 ) and leaf area index (LAI)-upscaled portable-photosynthesis-system transpiration estimates (R 2 = 0.88, RMSE = 0.06 mm h −1 ). Compared with the normal day, landscape ET was higher on the extreme-heat day, mainly reflecting higher tree transpiration (0.47 vs. 0.40 mm h −1 ), whereas grassland and shrub ET remained relatively stable. At the species level, three event-specific response groups were identified: enhanced with significantly higher transpiration under extreme heat (12 species), neutral with no significant change (3 species), and suppressed with significantly reduced transpiration (5 species). Random forest analysis identified the temperature vegetation dryness index (TVDI) and leaf-to-air vapor pressure deficit (VPD L ) as dominant controls of crown-scale transpiration, with tree height (TH) also exerting a strong influence. SHAP-derived tipping points for TH were identified at 7.01, 4.42, and 3.65 m in the enhanced, neutral, and suppressed response groups, respectively. SHAP-derived tipping points for TVDI (0.23–0.34) and VPD L (5.34–5.84 kPa) suggested the transition toward soil-water limitation and atmospheric-demand regulation. Overall, this framework enables spatially explicit assessment of urban tree water use and provides a basis for species selection and irrigation management during extreme heat.

title: Integrating Landsat and ECOSTRESS to explore the value of additional thermal infrared satellite observations for field-scale evapotranspiration mapping
summary: Landsat has provided an indispensable foundation for field-scale evapotranspiration (ET) mapping but is constrained by its overpass temporal frequency. Although integrating additional thermal data offers a pathway to bridge this gap, the magnitude of improvement varies across observation characteristics and surface context and remains less understood. Here, ECOsystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (ECOSTRESS) is used as an additional thermal source on top of the Landsat baseline to evaluate the value of more frequent thermal observations for improving field-scale ET time series. We implemented a Google Earth Engine -based Disaggregated Atmosphere-Land Exchange Inverse + Data Mining Sharpener framework to generate a Landsat-based ET baseline and enhanced it with ECOSTRESS observations. The resulting ET data was validated across 25 flux-tower sites spanning diverse land-cover types and climate zones across the contiguous United States. When integrated with Landsat, the addition of ECOSTRESS observations reduced interpolation errors and improved temporal consistency across most sites. However, improvements in ET time series agreement depended strongly on (1) the extent to which ECOSTRESS reduced effective Landsat sampling gaps and (2) the accuracy of overpass-day ECOSTRESS ET retrievals. Improvements were largest when ECOSTRESS shortened Landsat observation gaps by ~50% and maintained high scene quality. ECOSTRESS overpass time also influenced performance, with acquisitions between 10:00–14:00 producing most reliable ET estimates. These results support developing methods with multi-satellite observations to strengthen field-scale ET and help address the key knowledge gap regarding the value of increased thermal observations.

title: Twin-satellite constraints from GF-5B and DQ-1 enable hourly near-surface NO2 estimation across China
summary: Nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) is a major air pollutant with significant impacts on human health, yet satellite-based estimates of surface NO 2 with full diurnal coverage remain limited. Here, we develop a machine learning framework to estimate hourly near-surface NO 2 concentrations across China by integrating complementary observations from two Chinese polar-orbiting satellites, GF-5B (~10:30 local time) and DQ-1 (~13:30 local time). A Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model driven by twin-satellite NO 2 vertical column densities (VCDs) and meteorological reanalysis achieves strong predictive performance in 10-fold cross-validation, with a coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.91 and root mean square error (RMSE) of 5.40 μg/m 3 across all hours (4.46 μg/m 3 during daytime; 6.32 μg/m 3 at night), and retains reasonable skill under stricter site-based, time-based, and independent cross-year validation. The reconstructed dataset captures the characteristic diurnal cycle of NO 2 , with morning and evening peaks associated with traffic emissions and a midday minimum driven by photochemical loss. Compared to the single-satellite TROPOMI product, the twin-satellite configuration substantially improves the representation of diurnal variability, increasing R 2 from 0.81 to 0.91 and reducing RMSE by 31.60%, and corrects a distorted urban-rural NO 2 exposure ratio (1.70 for TROPOMI versus a ground-based 1.19), narrowing it to 1.30. Feature-importance analysis further shows that meteorological variables dominate model predictions during both day and night, with satellite VCDs providing a complementary, though indirect, constraint on nighttime concentrations. The resulting hourly NO 2 dataset demonstrates the value of synergistic multi-satellite observations for air quality monitoring and provides a robust basis for refined pollution control and population exposure assessment.

title: Advanced characterization of the diurnal variations of aerosol optical and microphysical properties by SYREMIS/GRASP synergistic retrieval algorithm using observations from multiple spaceborne sensors
summary: Accurate characterization of the diurnal variation of aerosol optical and microphysical properties—including Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), Angstrom Exponent (AE), and Single Scattering Albedo (SSA)—is fundamental for climate and air quality modeling. However, retrieving high-temporal-resolution, physically consistent aerosol products from multiple satellite instruments remains a challenge. Current multi-satellite approaches often rely on “post-retrieval” merging of independent Level-2 products, a process that frequently introduces physical inconsistencies and artificial temporal oscillations. To address this, building upon the recently established SYREMIS/GRASP synergetic retrieval framework (Litvinov et al., 2025), an inversion approach based on harmonized Level-1 satellite measurements, this study extensively evaluates its performance in capturing aerosol diurnal variability. We evaluate two configurations: (i) LEO + LEO synergy (Sentinel-3 A/B OLCI and Sentinel-5P TROPOMI) and (ii) LEO + GEO synergy (integrating Himawari-8 AHI). By enforcing multi-pixel smoothness constraints within the retrieval, SYREMIS maintains high physical consistency across instruments, effectively mitigating the structural discrepancies and “noise” inherent in standard merging techniques. Our validation against AERONET ground-based data and intercomparison with the XAERDT product suite confirm that SYREMIS provides high retrieval stability and accuracy. Without applying post-retrieval quality filtering, SYREMIS achieves an AOD GCOS fulfillment percentage of up to 70%, an AE RMSE below 0.3, and an SSA “Optimal” requirement fulfillment rate of up to 85% at representative sites. We demonstrate the framework's capability to resolve rapid aerosol dynamics through case studies of biomass-burning events over Thailand and Myanmar, as well as dust pollution over Qatar in 2019. As a three-month proof-of-concept assessment (March–May 2019) , these results highlight the practical capability of the established SYREMIS/GRASP approach to generate high-resolution, physically consistent, and stable aerosol data records from the measurements of multiple satellites.

title: Passive microwave sea ice concentration biases in the Southern Hemisphere revealed by ICESat-2 linear ice fraction
summary: Gridded sea ice concentration (SIC) data are fundamental for understanding long-term polar climate. Since 1978, daily SIC data have been derived from passive microwave (PM) satellite observations. As SIC is not directly observed, it is obtained through an algorithmic inversion of PM brightness temperatures. Differences between PM-SIC algorithms lead to uncertainty in SIC data. Here we examine differences between several PM-SIC products and focus primarily on two: the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) Climate Data Record (CDR), which over our study period is derived from Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) data, and over the Southern Ocean is largely based on the Bootstrap (BT) PM-SIC algorithm, and the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR2)-based NASATeam2 (NT2) product. On individual days, changes in integrated Antarctic sea ice area (SIA) can reach as high as 1.6 million km 2 in summer with relative differences up to 37% at the annual sea ice minimum. Using more than 1.8 million coincident observations of the ICESat-2 Linear Ice Fraction (LIF) from 2018 to 2024, we find BT-based PM-SIC data underestimate Antarctic SIC by a median of 0.2 in areas classified as the marginal ice zone (MIZ), corresponding to a median relative difference in SIC of 31%. This offset is seasonally, spatially, and parametrically consistent and yields differences in apparent MIZ extent as high as 4.4 million km 2 . The offset exceeds reported CDR uncertainties that average 0.07 and cannot be explained as a consequence of sensor differences. The parametric simplicity of the observed bias means these offsets can be parameterized as a function of BT SIC alone, which could lead to an improved SIC dataset for Antarctic studies.

title: A revised model for atmospheric adjacency effect correction in optical satellite earth observation images

title: Breaking modal barriers: Achieving modality-balanced semantic segmentation across optical and SAR images through optical image-supervised learning
summary: As the two primary imaging modalities in remote sensing, optics and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) have been widely applied in semantic segmentation tasks. However, the scarcity of annotated samples in SAR images limits the performance of related models. How to leverage the abundant annotated samples of optical images to achieve modality-balanced semantic segmentation capabilities across both optical and SAR modalities is of great significance for all-weather interpretation. Restricted by the complexity of modality perception, achieving balanced cross-modal segmentation still faces significant challenges. To address the above issues, we fully consider the modal balance and reliability of knowledge transfer in modal migration and propose a modality-balanced knowledge distillation (MBKD) transfer learning framework. By generating and learning virtual modalities and stitched modalities, a cross-modal migration task is transformed into two symmetric intra-modal migration subtasks, explicitly promoting balanced knowledge transfer between modalities. To demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed framework, we conducted application experiments on the large-scale public dataset WHU-OPT-SAR, MULTISENGE-6, and in 6 provinces of China. The results show that our method significantly outperforms other approaches in terms of both performance and stability.

title: GeoSeg-SAM: Task-aligned adaptation of SAM for geological remote sensing interpretation
summary: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) has shown strong performance in natural image segmentation. However, its direct transfer to geological environment remote sensing (GERS) is limited by significant domain discrepancies. GERS elements typically exhibit high class diversity, strong inter-class similarity, and imbalanced sample distribution, which challenge SAM’s prompt-driven paradigm in maintaining semantic stability and spatial contextual consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose GeoSeg-SAM, a geological task-aligned adaptation framework built upon SAM. GeoSeg-SAM progressively aligns generic visual features with geology-discriminative semantics through layer-wise semantic adapters, and introduces a dual-scale structure-aware module in the deeper encoder layers to enhance global region-level contextual representation. Meanwhile, the model employs Pyramid Residual Aggregation (PRA) to fuse multi-level geological semantic representations across stages, thereby improving the representational capacity of features. In addition, at the mask prediction stage, decoded features are fused with PRA-based semantic representations using a semantics-constrained fusion decoding strategy, and a single geological semantic token is incorporated to enhance semantic consistency in GERS scenarios. Experimental results on three representative GERS study areas show that GeoSeg-SAM improves mIoU by approximately 3 percentage points or more over the best competing method in each area, confirming its effectiveness in GERS image interpretation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/WanZhan-lucky/GeoSeg-SAM .

title: Assessing the spatio-temporal cumulative drought effects on two Mediterranean forest types in Central Chile
summary: Droughts are long-lasting events that can drive persistent functional changes in ecosystems, particularly in drought-prone areas like Mediterranean forests. We integrated a phenology-based anomaly method, combining kernel density estimation (KDE) with cumulative sums (CUSUMs) to assess long-term drought impacts on two Mediterranean forest types in Central Chile. Using MODIS Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), the Moisture Stress Index (MSI), and Evapotranspiration (ET) from 2000 to 2024, we quantified cumulative deviations in canopy productivity, moisture conditions, and energy exchange. Our framework revealed persistent negative functional trajectories preceding the well-documented 2010–present megadrought. Spatially explicit metrics identified coherent degradation hotspots in northern sclerophyllous and southern deciduous forests, where canopy greenness, moisture, and evapotranspiration declined synchronously. Seasonal models indicated a post-2010 strengthening of soil–water controls over forest functioning, with soil moisture and water storage variables becoming influential predictors. The convergence of cumulative negative EVI, MSI, and ET signals highlights widespread and sustained functional weakening under prolonged drought conditions. Our results demonstrate that integrating KDE-derived anomalies with cumulative deviation tracking provides a sensitive and transferable framework to detect early and persistent vegetation stress in water-limited ecosystems.

title: Prior-Informed Spatially Adaptive Network (PISA-Net) for multi-parameter water quality retrieval in Poyang Lake using Sentinel-2 imagery
summary: Accurate retrieval of water-quality parameters from remote-sensing imagery is essential for monitoring large inland lakes, yet pronounced spatial heterogeneity and limited transferability across varying environmental conditions remain major challenges. This study proposes a Prior-Informed Spatially Adaptive Network (PISA-Net) for multi-parameter water-quality retrieval from Sentinel-2 imagery in Poyang Lake. PISA-Net integrates a CNN branch for nonlinear spectral–spatial feature learning with a knowledge-guided branch based on empirical optical descriptors and coordinate-derived geographic priors. A geographic soft-assignment mechanism constructs the spatial prior vector, which conditions CNN features through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), while a stop gradient consistency loss (SG-CL) promotes agreement between the two prediction pathways with controlled gradient propagation. Chl-a, TP, and CODMn were modeled independently and evaluated using 5-fold spatial-block cross-validation against six representative empirical, statistical, machine-learning, and deep-learning baselines. PISA-Net achieved R 2 values of 0.6113, 0.5112, and 0.5054 for Chl-a, TP, and CODMn, respectively, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline, 2D-CNN, while reducing RMSE by approximately 29.6%, 21.4%, and 19.0%. An additional April 2018 cross-season experiment revealed substantial degradation under direct zero-shot transfer, whereas few-shot adaptation markedly reduced prediction errors, indicating useful cross-season adaptability after limited local calibration. Overall, PISA-Net provides a prior-informed spectral–spatial framework for water-quality retrieval under spatially heterogeneous conditions, while broader multi-season validation remains necessary to establish comprehensive seasonal generalizability.

title: Deep learning detection of submesoscale eddies from MODIS SST in the South China Sea
summary: Submesoscale eddies play crucial roles in oceanic energy cascades and material transport; however, their detection faces substantial challenges owing to inadequate spatial resolution in traditional satellite altimetric measurements. This research introduces Sub-Eddy-Net, an innovative deep learning approach utilizing an enhanced YOLOv8-SGAM architecture for identifying submesoscale eddy features within MODIS-derived sea surface temperature (SST) imagery across the South China Sea region. By exploiting SST data's advantageous temporal coverage and observational continuity relative to altimetric sensors, synthetic aperture radar, and ocean color products, the developed algorithm demonstrates detection precision of 0.968, successfully identifying 20,443 submesoscale eddies throughout 2015–2024. Results indicate cyclonic eddy prevalence exceeds anticyclonic occurrences, exhibiting average radii of 13.1 km and 13.7 km respectively. Eddy distributions primarily cluster within coastal waters and Luzon Strait vicinity, displaying pronounced seasonal patterns. Comparison with Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) observations shows 64.3% matched features, 27.1% positional offsets, and 8.6% detected only in SST. Within the same eddies, coherent chlorophyll-a (Chla) signatures were present in a smaller fraction, indicating that SST is the more robust tracer for systematic detection. This Sub-Eddy-Net methodology offers a scalable approach for examining submesoscale oceanic phenomena, providing a decadal inventory for further study of their roles in ocean circulation and vertical exchange.

title: A GeoAI framework for remote-sensing-driven traffic activity and emission intensity in a data-scarce megacity
summary: In rapidly expanding megacities across the Global South, a profound data scarcity paradox frequently prevents effective environmental monitoring and evidence driven urban planning. While severe traffic congestion generates acute localised pollution, the total absence of continuous municipal traffic counters, ubiquitous vehicle telemetry, and air quality monitoring networks leaves these environments empirically unmonitored. This study resolves this challenge by introducing a reproducible geocomputational framework designed to map microscale traffic activity and relative emission landscapes by fusing multisource geospatial data and deep learning workflows. Focusing on the unmonitored context of Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, our methodology uses very high resolution 15 cm satellite imagery to train and deploy a localised YOLOv8 (You Only Look Once, version 8) computer vision model, establishing an empirical baseline of fleet distribution. These static counts are dynamically distributed across the urban road network using a probabilistic Hub and Spoke Gravity Model, which is weighted through a zero shot Large Language Model semantic reclassification of unstructured OpenStreetMap features. Reconstructed kinematic flows are subsequently processed through velocity dependent Tier 3 EMEP/EEA algorithms to capture the nonlinear emission penalties triggered by severe network gridlock. To ensure framework defensibility, an independent unmanned aerial vehicle observation campaign was executed across ten distinct urban sites. The drone data directly validate model estimated physical parameters, achieving robust correlations for traffic volumes (R2 = 0.826) and link speeds (R2 = 0.925). Because literature derived chemical emission factors cannot be validated in situ, all absolute outputs are subjected to a rigorous multiparameter sensitivity analysis to report findings strictly as bounded ranges. The results reveal a clear structural handover in the spatial activity profile of the city. Daytime pollution is heavily driven by the informal paratransit fleet, which accounts for a bounded range of 82.8% to 95.1% of total PM2.5 emissions along primary corridors despite representing a numerical minority of active vehicles. Conversely, nocturnal baseline emissions transition to a landscape dominated almost entirely by private passenger vehicles. All code, processing pipelines, and validation datasets are available in a FAIR compliant open access repository. This framework establishes a scalable, remote sensing driven blueprint for diagnosing traffic activity structures in unmonitored metropolitan regions worldwide.

title: Integrating multi-source physical knowledge into deep learning for satellite soil moisture downscaling
summary: Fine-resolution soil moisture (SM) is essential for understanding land–atmosphere interactions and managing hydrological hazards at local scales. Passive microwave remote sensing provides reliable SM observations but is limited by its coarse spatial resolution. Spatial downscaling offers an important means of addressing this limitation. However, many existing downscaling methods either rely on physical models with over-simplifications of soil hydrological knowledge, or data-driven models (particularly Deep Learning, DL) that lack interpretability, while current physics-guided DL approaches often emphasize a limited number of physical relationships or constraints. In response, this study proposes a framework to integrate multi-source physical knowledge into DL for satellite SM downscaling. Specifically, the framework incorporates physically informed drivers, a DisPATCh-informed physical regression branch, a hydrologically motivated consistency loss, and a constrained SM boundary loss, while using a gating module to adaptively fuse physically guided and data-driven representations. Evaluations based on in-situ and aircraft SM observations, together with coarse-scale consistency checks against SMAP SM, show that the proposed framework can effectively downscale SMAP SM from 9 km to 500 m. Using region-specific models across ten environmentally diverse regions, MPhy achieved station-averaged Pearson’s R and ubRMSE values of 0.76 and 0.05 m3/m3, respectively; the corresponding values for the pure-DL baseline Dens were 0.68 and 0.06 m3/m3. Detailed experiments in WGEW further showed that MPhy generally performed better than the pure-DL baseline, DisPATCh, single-physics-informed models, and selected conventional machine-learning methods. Overall, the results support improved physical plausibility and convergence efficiency, as well as framework robustness across the evaluated environments.

title: Adaptive smooth constrained stereo matching and disparity refinement for satellite DSM generation
summary: High-resolution satellite images often exhibit substantial geometric and radiometric differences, making it difficult for conventional stereo matching methods to achieve high matching accuracy while suppressing noise and preserving object boundaries. To address this issue, this study improves both stereo matching and disparity post-processing in the satellite digital surface model (DSM) generation workflow. First, within the semi-global matching (SGM) framework, a mixed matching cost is constructed by combining the Census transform and gradient descriptors. Image gradients and edge cues extracted by a pretrained PiDiNet are then incorporated to adaptively control the strength of the smoothness constraint during cost aggregation, thereby improving matching reliability while balancing noise suppression and disparity-boundary preservation. Second, we propose a disparity post-processing method that combines improved weighted least-squares disparity refinement with matching-cost-based disparity fusion. The method first dynamically adjusts the smoothing weights to reduce texture-copying artifacts and edge blurring and then fuses disparity using matching costs to alleviate staircase artifacts caused by excessive smoothing. Experiments were conducted on ZY3-02 and WorldView-3 satellite imagery, with SGM, S2P-HD, Agisoft Metashape software, guided aggregation net, and FoundationStereo included for comparison. Across three test scenes dominated by urban and agricultural areas, the proposed method increased the proportion of pixels with absolute elevation errors below 2 m by an average of 4.12 percentage points and reduced RMSE by an average of 0.11 m compared with standard SGM. Qualitative results further show that the proposed method effectively suppresses noise in relatively flat regions while preserving building boundaries.

title: A large-scale spatiotemporal NDVI prediction method coupling multivariable constraints and structured modeling
summary: Accurate prediction of vegetation dynamics is essential for understanding terrestrial ecosystems carbon and water cycles. However, existing Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) prediction methods are limited in their ability to represent spatiotemporal heterogeneity and nonlinear interactions among multiple driving variables, which restrict predictive accuracy and extrapolation performance at large scales. To address these limitations, this study proposed a structured large-scale NDVI spatiotemporal prediction method incorporating multivariable constraints (MCS-LSTP) to characterize vegetation dynamics in complex and heterogeneous environments. MCS-LSTP incorporates multiple key driving variables and enhances the comprehensive representation of complex spatiotemporal dependencies and spatial heterogeneity through homogeneous spatial unit partitioning, unit-level temporal modeling, and continuous surface reconstruction. Results showed that MCS-LSTP model exhibited superior performance in terms of stability and prediction accuracy when compared to AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Random Forest (RF), and Transformer models. The mean Population Stability Index (PSI) reached 0.0572, with 98.7% of prediction units exhibiting PSI values below 0.1, indicating no significant deviation between the observed and simulated NDVI values. The average R2 and RMSE on the test set were 0.8551 and 0.2171, respectively. Furthermore, MCS-LSTP accurately reproduced seasonal NDVI fluctuations and meridional spatial gradients, with particularly high agreement between simulated and reference values during the growing season. This study provides a robust and scalable solution for large-scale NDVI spatiotemporal prediction and offers critical technical support for ecological risk assessment in the Yellow River Basin and other ecologically vulnerable regions.

title: Transforming Leaf-Off LiDAR to leaf-on canopy height models using deep learning
summary: Accurate tree canopy metrics are essential for a wide range of ecological, environmental, and climate studies. Recent advances in airborne LiDAR sensing have greatly expanded access to high-resolution three-dimensional observations of tree canopy structure. However, many widely available airborne LiDAR datasets are acquired under leaf-off conditions to support terrain mapping, and our analysis across ecologically diverse sites shows that canopy height models (CHMs) derived from these data exhibit substantial, recurring discrepancies in canopy height and extent, with an overall tendency to underrepresent canopy structure relative to leaf-on conditions. These discrepancies limit the direct use of leaf-off CHMs in applications requiring canopy information representative of leaf-on conditions. To address this limitation, we introduce a deep learning framework for reconstructing leaf-on CHMs from existing leaf-off LiDAR-derived CHMs. To our knowledge, this is the first study to formulate the direct reconstruction of leaf-on CHMs from existing leaf-off LiDAR-derived CHMs as a supervised image-to-image learning task. The framework provides two complementary models: a Pix2Pix model that uses the leaf-off CHM alone and a U-Net model that additionally incorporates multispectral imagery. Our proposed models achieve robust canopy-height accuracy across four spatially independent test sites (R²: 0.85–0.92; Mean Absolute Error: 1.3–1.6 metres), substantially reducing the discrepancies observed in the leaf-off source CHMs. They also provide sharper delineation of canopy details and higher accuracy than recent optical-imagery-based approaches. To facilitate broader use, we developed an open-access web application that deploys the pre-trained models and supports on-demand leaf-on CHM generation for user-selected areas across the U.S. where suitable leaf-off LiDAR inputs are available. Overall, the framework provides a practical means to bridge the seasonal data gap in LiDAR acquisition and improve access to reliable canopy metrics representative of leaf-on conditions.
